title: Mihrab and minbar
hook: the niche shows the qiblah; the steps are where the Friday sermon is given

segments.voice: Yesterday: the washing place, the room of low taps near the door. Your line was wash, then enter. Did you walk into something fresh? Day one hundred forty.

You've washed. Shoes are off. You step into the prayer hall, and the first surprise is how empty it is. No pews. No altar. No statues. Mostly carpet, often with lines woven into it. But look at the far wall. There's a curved niche set into it, sometimes plain, sometimes covered in tiles and calligraphy. And just to its right, a small staircase that leads nowhere, with a little platform at the top. Two pieces of furniture in a nearly empty room. Each has a job. Today: mihrab and minbar.
screen: `NO PEWS, NO ALTAR, NO STATUES.` → `A CURVED NICHE IN THE WALL.` → `STAIRS THAT LEAD NOWHERE.`

segments.voice: The niche is the mihrab. Its job is simple: it marks the qiblah, the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca, which you met on day ninety-nine. Walk into any mosque in the world, look for the mihrab, and you know which way everyone will face. The imam who leads the prayer stands in front of it, and in many mosques its curve helps carry his voice back into the room. The word itself is old. The Qur'an uses it in the story of Maryam, the mother of Isa: whenever Zakariyya came to her in the mihrab, her place of prayer, he found food with her, and asked where it came from. In the Prophet's own mosque there was no niche at all; historians say the curved mihrab came a few generations later, when that mosque was rebuilt. The staircase is the minbar, the pulpit, where the imam gives the sermon at the Friday prayer. And its story is one of the most tender in Bukhari. At first, the Prophet ﷺ gave his sermons leaning against the trunk of a palm tree. Then a minbar of three wooden steps was made for him. The first Friday he climbed it, the companions heard the old palm trunk cry out, like a child, or like a camel longing for its young. The Prophet came down, and put his hand on it, and held it until it went quiet. The mihrab says where to face. The minbar says who will speak. But neither is holy in itself. What they do together is point a whole room one way, so that the rich man and the cleaner, the old and the new, face the same way.
screen: `MIHRAB — THE NICHE THAT SHOWS THE QIBLAH.` · `MARYAM IN THE MIHRAB.` · `MINBAR — THE STEPS FOR THE SERMON.` · `THE PALM TRUNK THAT CRIED.` · then, large: `EVERYONE FACES THE SAME WAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice where a room points. Look around the room you're in. Every room faces somewhere: toward a screen, a window, a desk, a door. Where do the chairs point? Where does your body turn by default? Now, if you know it, turn to face the direction of Mecca, or just toward a window, somewhere with light. Sit, and let your whole body face one way. If other people are near, notice that you could all be facing the same way without saying a word. The bell holds the time.
Mihrab. The niche in a mosque's front wall that shows the qiblah, the direction everyone faces in prayer. Today's word.

Your line: everyone faces the same way. Once today, in a line, a meeting or a crowd, notice that you're all facing the same way, and let that make you a little kinder to the person beside you. Day one hundred forty.

howItsDone: In the mosque the imam leads the prayer standing before the mihrab, the niche marking the qiblah, and gives the Friday sermon from the minbar, a stepped pulpit beside it.

fork.reveal: Bukhari reports he came down and held the trunk until it went quiet. one of the most tender stories in the collection.

original.note: Arabic: the niche that marks the qiblah; the Qur'an uses the word for Maryam's place of prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: the fancy arch is the mosque's altar.
what it means: the mihrab only marks which way to face, and the minbar beside it is where the sermon is given.
what a scholar hears: mihrab in 3:37; the concave mihrab dated to the Umayyad rebuilding of Medina; the weeping trunk (Bukhari 3583).

sources.ref: Qur'an 3:37 (Zakariyya finds food with Maryam in the mihrab)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3583, 3584 (the palm trunk that cried)
Sahih al-Bukhari 917 (the minbar of tamarisk wood)

notes: Hadith numbers cited from memory; please confirm.
Dating of the concave mihrab to the Umayyad-era rebuilding of the Prophet's mosque (c. 707–709, under Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz as governor) is the common historical account; confirm.
'Its curve helps carry his voice' is commonly said; soften if not wanted.
The minbar's position (to the right of the mihrab, as seen facing it) is typical but not universal.
